title: Filling in the blanks
text:
For the rest of the numbers up to 99, they follow a consistent pattern. For example, thirty-one is simply **treinta y uno** (*literally, thirty and one*) and forty-five is **cuarenta y cinco** (*literally, forty and five*).

---

This simple pattern continues all the way to 99, without any exceptions. Finally, one rule without exception!

---

31\. treinta y uno
32\. treinta y dos
33\. treinta y tres
34\. treinta y cuatro
35\. treinta y cinco
36\. treinta y seis

---

37\. treinta y siete
38\. treinta y ocho
39\. treinta y nueve
40\. cuarenta
41\. cuarenta y uno
42\. cuarenta y dos... 
and so on, up to 99.

---

The easy way to remember this is that from thirty up, you use this formula: *tens number* + **y** + *single digit number*.

Easy peasy!

title: Hello, goodbye
text:
Let's go over a few of the key greetings you'll need right away, just to say hello and goodbye.

There are, of course, lots of others, including slang and regional words, we'll encounter those as we go. For now, let's focus on the basics.

---

|  **Spanish**  |  **English**  | 
| --------- | -------- |
| **hola**  | hello |
| **adiós**  | goodbye |
| **hasta pronto**  | see you soon *(lit: until soon)* |
| **hasta luego**  | see you later *(lit: until later)* |
| **nos vemos**  | see you later *(lit: we'll see each other)* |
| **buenos días**  | good morning |
| **buenas tardes**  | good afternoon |
| **buenas noches**  | good evening, good night |

---

Note that **hasta luego** and **nos vemos** are fairly interchangeable. Both serve the purpose of saying "I'll see you later," they're just two different ways of communicating the same thing.

**Hasta luego** literally means "until later," while **nos vemos** means "we'll see each other."

title: Hello, my name is...
text:
When learning a new language, one of the most important things to be able to do early on is to introduce yourself. Let's learn a basic way to say hello and tell someone your name in Spanish!

---

**María:** Hola, ¿cómo estás?
**Jorge:** Bien, ¿y tú?
**María:** Muy bien, gracias. ¿Cómo te llamas?
**Jorge:** Soy Jorge. ¿Y tú?
**María:** Me llamo María. Mucho gusto, Jorge.
**Jorge:** Mucho gusto.

title: Hopes and dreams
text:
All right, so we know how to conjugate the subjunctive now, but when should we use it?

The first case is when expressing a **desire** or **wish**.

---

Earlier on, we said that the subjunctive was used in cases of *uncertainty*. When expressing a desire, there is an inherent element of uncertainty. We're *hoping* that something happens, but we can't be *absolutely certain* that it will.

---

In this case, sentences often break out into two clauses, one indicative and one subjunctive. The indicative clause reports what it is the speaker is doing (hoping, wanting, suggesting, etc.), while the subjunctive clause tells us what the speaker is hoping for, something that has not yet happened and is therefore uncertain.

---
Take this sentence, for example: I hope **that my sister goes to the store**.

The first clause (*I hope*) is indicative because I am certain that I am *hoping* for something. It's a fact. However, I'm not certain of what my sister will do. I may *really want* her to go to the store, but until she does, I can't report it as a fact. There's an element of uncertainty.

---

Here are a few more examples that show where we use the indicative and where we use the subjunctive.

I hope **that he speaks Spanish**.

The doctor wants **his patients to be healthy**.

I prefer **that you play outside**.

The teacher suggests **that the student read the book**.

---

To put it in simple terms, the subject's action uses the indicative mood, while the outcome they desire uses the subjunctive. Let's see the previous sentences with their Spanish translations.

**Espero que él hable español.**
*I hope that he speaks Spanish.*

**El doctor quiere que sus pacientes estén sanos.**
*The doctor wants his patients to be healthy.*

---

**Prefiero que juegues afuera.**
*I prefer that you play outside.*

**La maestra sugiere que el estudiante lea el libro.**
*The teacher suggests that the student read the book.*

---

Here are a few *desire* words that will likely be paired with a subjunctive clause.

- esperar - to hope
- querer - to want
- preferir - to prefer
- insistir - to insist (on)
- recomendar - to recommend
- sugerir - to suggest

---

Two important notes here:

1. This list is far from exhaustive. Part of the tricky nature of the subjunctive is that it's not always clear when exactly to use it. The rule of thumb is that if there's any element of uncertainty, something outside your control that you can't report as an absolute fact, then the subjunctive would likely be appropriate.

---

2. Most of the verbs in this *desire* section are paired with **que** (*that*), as in "I hope that..." or "She insists that..."

You'll see this more in practice. Speaking of practice, let's get to it!

title: I don't know the meaning
text:
The past participle is a fairly simple and quite useful verb form. It's something you likely use every day in English, though the name might sound unfamiliar.

For this lesson, we'll be talking about its use as an adjective, and later in the unit, we'll dive into how it can be combined with another verb to create the perfect tense.

---

In English, you can think of the past participle as the **-ed** form of a verb, as it's often conjugated by adding **-ed** or **-d** to the end of a verb in English.

For example, *constructed*, *brushed*, *opened*, and *closed* are all past participles.

---

Of course, English being English, there are almost more exceptions than rules, as some more examples will illustrate: *written*, *driven*, *broken*, *seen*, *built*.

*Note: Though some of these conjugations are the same as the regular past tense (particularly the **-ed** ones), the past participle is distinct from the past tense (saw vs. seen, wrote vs. written)*

---

To conjugate the past participle in Spanish, we remove the infinitive ending (-ar, -er, or -ir) and add **-ado** to -ar verbs, or **-ido** to -er and -ir verbs.

---

Here are a few examples:

**cerrar** -> **cerrado**
*to close* -> *closed*

**construir** -> **construido**
*to build* -> *built*

---

Alone, a past participle can be used as an adjective. For example: 

**El restaurante está cerrado.**
*The restaurant is closed.*

**La casa está terminada.**
*The house is finished.*

**El juguete perdido**
*The lost toy*

---

Just like all other adjectives, the past participle has to match up to the noun it's modifying or describing in both gender and plurality.

El restaurante está **cerrado**.
*The restaurant is closed.*

La ventana está **cerrada**.
*The window is closed.*

Los cines están **cerrados**.
*The movie theaters are closed.*

Las puertas están **cerradas**.
*The doors are closed.*

---

Remember that using the past participle as an adjective is just one of several uses that we'll discuss throughout this unit.

title: I feel incomplete
text:
As we established when talking about desire, actions that are not yet completed have an inherent degree of uncertainty, as we can't be *absolutely sure* that they will come to pass.

---

These *uncompleted action* sentences usually have an element of time (**when** the action is completed, something will happen) or a condition (**if** the action is completed, something will happen).

---

The first parts of our examples here are the indicative clauses, as we are making the objective statement that something will happen. The second, bolded parts are the subjunctive clauses, relying on the assumption that the action will take place.

---

Let's look at some more concrete examples:

I will read the book **as soon as he finishes it**.
*I will certainly read the book, assuming he finishes reading it first.*

My brother will watch TV **while I cook dinner**.
*My brother will watch for sure, as long as I actually cook dinner.*

---

There are a few key phrases that let us know we're talking about an uncompleted action. These ones each have a conditional element:

- **a menos que** - unless
- **en caso de que** - in case
- **con tal (de) que** - provided that

---

And these have an element of time:

- **antes (de) que** - before
- **después (de) que** - after
- **mientras que** - while
- **hasta que** - until
- **tan pronto como** - as soon as

---

The key takeaway here is that all these phrases contain either an element of time or a condition. In other words, they rely on the uncompleted action being completed before the statement will come true.

---

This rule can help guide as you determine whether you should use the subjunctive out there in the real world. But until then, let's practice!

title: I seriously doubt that
text:
The second main way we use the subjunctive is when expressing doubt, which, by its definition, has an element of uncertainty.

---

Just like when talking about desire, there are a few key verb phrases that give us a clue that we should use the subjunctive. Here are a few of the most common:

- **dudar** - to doubt
- **no creer** - to not believe
- **no estar seguro** - to not be sure
- **no pensar** - to not think
- **no estar convencido** - to not be convinced

---

Notice all of these verbs (except for *dudar*) are only used as negatives in relation to the subjunctive. If we were to use the positive, we would actually use the *indicative* mood.

For example, while **No creo que...** (*I don't believe that...*) has an element of doubt and uncertainty, **Creo que...** (*I believe that...*) is quite the opposite, showing that we're sure of something.

---

In addition to these verbs, there are a few other statements that indicate the use of the subjunctive:

- **es dudoso que** - it is doubtful that
- **es improbable que** - it’s unlikely/improbable that
- **es posible que** - it’s possible that

---

We could put a much longer list of examples here, but these are the most key phrases that will let you know the subjunctive should be coming up in the following clause.

You know the rules now, so use your best judgment: any phrase that introduces an element of doubt or ignorance (not being totally sure of something) should be paired with the subjunctive.

---

For other specific examples, we'll just have to practice and see them in use!

title: I would've gotten away with it, too
If it weren't for you meddling kids!
I'm not in the mood
text:
This unit is all about the subjunctive. With the subjunctive, we're leaving the comfort of the **tense** and venturing into the unknown world of the **mood**.

Okay, it's not that unknown. We technically have the subjunctive in English too, and it'll sound pretty familiar to you start working with it. We'll try to keep it simple.

---

First of all, what's the difference between a *tense* and a *mood*? At the most basic level, a *tense* lets us know when something is taking place (past, present, future, ongoing, etc.), while a *mood* expresses how the speaker feels about an action.

---

We've been using only one mood up to this point: the **indicative**. The indicative mood is used to report or declare something that is objective or certain, as well as to ask questions. It's the most commonly used mood, and should be your default.

For example:

**Yo sé que eres estudiante.**
*I know that you are a student.*

**¿Quieres ir al cine?**
*Do you want to go to the movie theater?*

---

In contrast, the **subjunctive** mood is used for *subjectivity*, anything that's not certain or objective. This includes things like desires, opinions, and uncertainty.

**Espero qué él hable inglés.**
*I hope that he speaks English.*

**Ella quiere que su hijo la llame.**
*She wants her son to call her.*

---

So, when deciding whether to use the indicative or the subjunctive, you can think of it in very simple terms:

certainty and objectivity = **indicative**

uncertainty and subjectivity = **subjunctive**

---

That's the main gist of it, but of course we'll give you some examples throughout this pack of when exactly you should use the subjunctive.

Broadly, the subjunctive fits into these situations:

1. Desire
2. Doubt
3. Uncompleted actions
4. Impersonal opinions

---

First things first, let's learn how to conjugate the subjunctive and use it to express our desires!

title: Imperfection
text:
We previously learned how to talk about completed, definite actions in the past using the **preterite** form, but there's another form of past tense in Spanish called the **imperfect**. 

---

The **imperfect** is used for actions that occurred in the past but are either:
1. not seen as being completed or finished, and/or
2. do not have a definite beginning and end.

Let's take a look at the different uses for the imperfect tense with some practical examples.

---

*Note: we'll talk about the conjugations of all these verbs throughout this unit, but this lesson is just using examples to illustrate the cases where we would use the imperfect. So don't worry if the conjugations look a little strange right now, they'll all make sense soon.*

---

**Things you used to do**

The imperfect tense is used to talk about past actions that were habitual or recurring, meaning that they happened more than once, most likely at a semi-regular interval.

In English, this will often translate as something that one "used to do" or "would do" in the past.

---

Here are a few examples:

**Comíamos juntos cada día.**
*We used to eat together every day.*

**Hablabamos en la escuela.**
*We used to talk in school.*

---

**Past dates and times**

We also use the imperfect to speak about dates and times in the past.

**Eran las once de la noche.**
*It was eleven at night.*

**Era el cuatro de julio.**
*It was the fourth of July.*

---

**How old you were**

The imperfect can be used to talk about how old someone was at a point in the past.

**Yo tenía diez años.**
*I was ten years old.*

**Los elefantes tenían tres años.**
*The elephants were three years old.*

title: Increasing irregularity
text:
The next two verbs we'll look at are **decir** *(to say)* and **hacer** *(to do)*. Here's a quick trick to make sense of the next chart: imagine that the *infinitives* for these verbs (the dictionary forms ending in -ir and -er) change before they are conjugated.

---

In other words, imagine that *decir* becomes **dijir** and *hacer* becomes **hicer**. Then, if you conjugate those new made-up infinitives using the regular rules for the preterite, you'll have everything correct!

---

*Note: we don't recommend actually memorizing these imaginary infinitives, as that could get confusing, but if it helps you conjugate the verbs in this form, feel free to use them! Otherwise, just forget we ever said anything about it.*

---

*Second note: pay special attention to the singular third person (él/ella) form for **hacer**, which becomes **hizo** in the preterite, thanks to the sound-changing rules for Spanish.*

---

|  **Pronoun**  |  **decir** *(to say)*  |  **hacer** *(to do)*  | 
| --------- | -------- | -------- |
| **yo**  | dije | hice |
| **tú** | dijiste | hiciste |
| **él/ella** | dijo | hizo | 
| **nosotros/nosotras** | dijimos | hicimos |
| **ellos/ellas** | dijeron | hicieron |

---

Here are a couple of examples:

**¿Qué dijiste?**
*What did you say?*

**Hice toda la tarea.**
*I did all of the homework.*

---

As a bonus for this lesson, let's quickly learn how **ver** *(to see)* works in the preterite, mainly because it's nothing too crazy:

|  **Pronoun**  |  **ver** *(to see)*  | 
| --------- | -------- |
| **yo**  | vi |
| **tú** | viste |
| **él/ella** | vio | 
| **nosotros/nosotras** | vimos |
| **ellos/ellas** | vieron |

---

You might look at that chart and think, "Wait, what's irregular about that? It looks completely normal!"

Don't worry, we did the same thing. Essentially, the only irregular thing about **ver** is that it doesn't use the accented characters. So instead of **ví** and **vió** (which it would normally be), we get **vi** and **vio**.

title: Indefinite action - the imperfect
text:
The **imperfect** is used for actions that occurred in the past but are either:
1. not seen as being completed or finished, and/or
2. do not have a definite beginning and end

---

Often the imperfect can be translated into English as something that someone *used to do* or *would do* in the past. Here are a couple examples:

**Leíamos libros.**
*We used to read books.*
*We would read books.*

**Hablaban juntos.**
*They used to talk together.*
*They would talk together.*

---

*Note: you can also translate the imperfect as the regular past tense, just be aware that it carries the connotation of an action that used to happen (specifically, more than once), but no longer does.*

---

Here are the **past tense** conjugation charts using the **imperfect** form for regular verbs:

|  **Pronoun**  |  **Ending**  | 
| --------- | -------- |
| **yo**  | -aba |
| **tú** | -abas |
| **él/ella** | -aba | 
| **nosotros/nosotras** | -abamos |
| **ellos/ellas** | -aban |

---

The -er and -ir verb endings look quite different from the -ar verbs, but are (fortunately) the same as each other. This chart applies to *both* -er and -ir verbs.

|  **Pronoun**  |  **Ending**  | 
| --------- | -------- |
| **yo**  | -ía |
| **tú** | -ías |
| **él/ella** | -ía | 
| **nosotros/nosotras** | -íamos |
| **ellos/ellas** | -ían |

---

Here are some fully conjugated examples for each of the verb groups:

|  **Spanish**  |  **English**  | 
| --------- | -------- |
| **hablar**  | to speak |
| **(yo) hablaba** | I spoke |
| **(tú) hablabas** | you spoke |
| **(él/ella) hablaba** | he/she spoke | 
| **(nosotros) hablabamos** | we spoke |
| **(ellos) hablaban** | they spoke |

---

|  **Spanish**  |  **English**  | 
| --------- | -------- |
| **comer**  | to eat |
| **(yo) comía** | I ate |
| **(tú) comías** | you ate |
| **(él/ella) comía** | he/she ate | 
| **(nosotros) comíamos** | we ate |
| **(ellos) comían** | they ate |

---

|  **Spanish**  |  **English**  | 
| --------- | -------- |
| **escribir**  | to write |
| **(yo) escribía** | I wrote |
| **(tú) escribías** | you wrote |
| **(él/ella) escribía** | he/she wrote | 
| **(nosotros) escribíamos** | we wrote |
| **(ellos) escribían** | they wrote |

title: Informal vs. simple
text:
Now that we know how to use both the **informal future** and the **simple future**, we need to understand when we should use each one. 

Let's talk about the context for using these two different methods.

---

You can think of the informal future (*ir + a + infinitive*) as covering any action that's going to happen in the **relatively near future**.

**Voy a viajar a Japón el próximo mes.**
*I'm going to travel to Japan next month.*

**Él va a beber cerveza.**
*He is going to drink beer.*

**El estudiante va a estudiar español.**
*The student is going to study Spanish.*

---

Essentially, if what you want to say in English begins with "I'm going to...", you can use the informal future. This is by far the more common way to express things you're going to do in everyday life.

---

The **simple future**, in contrast, is used for actions that will take place further in the future.

**Viajaré a Colombia el año que viene.**
*I'll travel to Colombia next year.*

**Después de la universidad, él será un doctor.**
*After university, he'll be a doctor.*

---

The **simple future** is also used in cases where you want to express curiosity without asking a direct, pointed question in the present tense. In English, these kinds of sentences can be translated in multiple ways, meaning essentially the same thing and having the same connotation of curiosity.

---

Take a look at these examples of expressing curiosity with the simple future:

**¿Quién será eso?**
*Who could that be?*
*I wonder who that is.*

**¿Dónde estarán los niños?**
*Where could the children be?*
*I wonder where the children are.*

---

The third—and final—primary use of the **simple future** is to talk about probability:

**Ella estará estudiando.**
*She is probably studying.*

**Ellos comerá pescado.**
*They probably eat fish.*

---

Keep in mind that there are other ways to express curiosity and probability (using words like **preguntarse** (*to wonder*) and **probablamente** (*probably*)), but as this is one key use of the **simple future** that differentiates it from the **informal future**, we wanted to introduce it here.

---

To review: the **informal future** is the more commonly used form, and it generally refers to actions happening in the relatively near future.

The **simple future** is used for events further out, as well as to express curiosity and probability regarding current situations and actions.

title: Irregular, as always
text:
As per usual, there are a number of important verbs that are irregular in the past participle. Let's look at a few of the ones you'll see most often.

---

**abrir** -> **abierto**
*to open* -> *opened*

**cubrir** -> **cubierto**
*to cover* -> *covered*

**decir** -> **dicho**
*to say* -> *said*

---

**escribir** -> **escrito**
*to write* -> *written*

**hacer** -> **hecho**
*to do* -> *done*

**ver** -> **visto**
*to see* -> *seen*

---

**romper** -> **roto**
*to break* -> *broken*

**morir** -> **muerto**
*to die* -> *dead*

**volver** -> **vuelto**
*to return* -> *returned*

---

There aren't any solid rules around forming these irregular past participles, so they're just ones you'll have to memorize. Don't worry, we'll see them quite a bit as we practice!

title: Irregular, but useful
text:
Even though Spanish verbs have a lot of conjugations, they're great in that most of them are regular and follow the rules, so we just need to know the root and can conjugate any form from there.

However, there are some really important basic verbs we haven't talked about yet, because they're irregular.

---

It's definitely annoying that these are some of the verbs you'll use most often in conversation, and yet they don't follow the rules, so you have to just memorize their conjugations (like **tener**—*to have*—which we went over earlier).

---

Fortunately, they're often at least *similar* to the regular conjugations, with just slight changes.

And because you'll use these often, you should have no trouble getting them down simply by using them! Let's go over a couple here, and then we'll circle back for more.

---

|  **Spanish**  |  **English**  | 
| --------- | -------- |
| **querer**  | to want |
| **(yo) quiero** | I want |
| **(tú) quieres** | you want |
| **(él/ella) quiere** | he/she wants | 
| **(nosotros) queremos** | we want |
| **(ellos) quieren** | they want |

---

|  **Spanish**  |  **English**  | 
| --------- | -------- |
| **hacer**  | to do |
| **(yo) hago** | I do |
| **(tú) haces** | you do |
| **(él/ella) hace** | he/she does | 
| **(nosotros) hacemos** | we do |
| **(ellos) hacen** | they do |

*Note: hacer also means "to make"*

---

|  **Spanish**  |  **English**  | 
| --------- | -------- |
| **decir**  | to say |
| **(yo) digo** | I say |
| **(tú) dices** | you say |
| **(él/ella) dice** | he/she says | 
| **(nosotros) decimos** | we say |
| **(ellos) dicen** | they say |

title: Irregular orders
text:
As you've probably gotten used to by now, there are a few important verbs that have irregular imperative forms. These ones should look familiar, as we've seen them many times before.

---

|  **English** |  **Infinitive**  |  **Imperative**  | 
| --------- | -------- | -------- |
| to say | decir | **di** |
| to do | hacer | **haz** |
| to go | ir | **ve** |
| to come | venir | **ven** |
| to leave | salir | **sal** |
| to have | tener | **ten** |
| to put | poner | **pon** |
| to be | ser | **sé** |

---
	
Keep in mind that this irregularity only applies in the *positive*. If you're telling someone *not* to do something, we stick with the **second-person subjunctive**, just like we use for all the regular verbs.

---

| **Infinitive**  |  **Negative Imperative**  | 
| -------- | -------- |
| decir | **no digas** |
| hacer | **no hagas** |
| ir | **no vayas** |
| venir | **no vengas** |
| salir | **no salgas** |
| tener | **no tengas** |
| poner | **no pongas** |
| ser | **no seas** |

---

Okey dokey, amigos, let's practice!

title: It takes two to tengo
text:
We've been looking at the three main groups of regular verbs so far, but it's time to tackle our first *irregular* verb (well, other than **ser**, which we've already covered).

---

The first one we'll discuss is **tener** (*to have*). Unfortunately, because it's irregular, you'll just have to memorize its conjugations. However, since it's a verb you'll use so often, it shouldn't take you long to have them down solid!

---

Here are the conjugations for **tener** in the present tense:

|  **Spanish**  |  **English**  | 
| --------- | -------- |
| **tener**  | to have |
| **(yo) tengo** | I have |
| **(tú) tienes** | you have |
| **(él/ella) tiene** | he/she has | 
| **(nosotros) tenemos** | we have |
| **(ellos) tienen** | they have |
| **(ustedes) tienen** | you (all) have |

title: It would be irregular
text:
As with most of the other tenses, there are a few key verbs that are irregular in the conditional. In this case, the *endings* that we've learned stay the same while the *infinitive* changes.

---

These irregular conjugations fit neatly into two groups (with two left over), so let's take a look at these one at a time. We'll cover the first group in this lesson.

---

In the first group, we simply remove the last vowel in the verb and add the proper conditional ending. 

For example, **saber** (*to know*) would become **sabría** in the first and third person.

---

Let's take a look at each conjugation for **saber** before looking at the other verbs in this group:

|  **Spanish**  |  **English**  | 
| --------- | -------- |
| **saber**  | to know |
| **(yo) sabría** | I would know |
| **(tú) sabrías** | you would know |
| **(él/ella) sabría** | he/she would know | 
| **(nosotros) sabríamos** | we would know |
| **(ellos) sabrían** | they would know |

---

Here are all the verbs in this first group:

|  **Infinitive**  | **Meaning** | **Conditional**  | 
| --------- | -------- | -------- |
| saber  | to know | **sabría** |
| poder  | to be able to | **podría** |
| caber  | to fit | **cabría** |
| haber  | to have/to exist | **habría** |

---

Let's practice this first group before moving on to the rest!

title: It's absolutely imperative
text:
Sometimes, you just need to tell someone do something. This is often referred to as either a **command** or an **imperative** (either is fine), and that's what we'll be learning in this unit.

---

If you have a background in Spanish (or are just very observant), you may have noticed that we've been focusing mostly on *informal* or *familiar speech*. In the most basic terms, this means using **tú** instead of **usted** when speaking to someone.

---

Most grammar textbooks will put an emphasis on learning to use **usted** from the very beginning, but it turns out that this type of *formal speech* is less common in reality, and you're better off defaulting to informal speech.

We want you to start using your Spanish quickly, rather than get confused between different forms and which you should use at any given time.

---

We're bringing this up now because it applies especially clearly to commands. There is a distinction in conjugation between formal and informal commands, but as we've been doing so far, we're going to save some of that complexity for later.

---

All right, now that we have that out of the way, how do we actually use the imperative? It's pretty simple, actually.

In English, we use the third-person present form of a verb to issue a command (**run** there, **eat** this, **give** it to me, etc.), and we do the exact same in Spanish.

---

So, you use the same verb conjugation you would use when talking about **él** or **ella** to tell someone to do something:

**Toma la foto.**
*Take the photo.*

**Come la comida.**
*Eat the food.*

**Escribe el libro.**
*Write the book.*

---

Before we talk about how to tell someone to *not* do something, let's practice telling them what *to* do!

title: It's in the past
text:
Unlike English, Spanish has two past tenses. These are called the **preterite** and the **imperfect**.

Simply put, the **preterite** is used for actions that are completed, that have a definite beginning and end, while the **imperfect** is used for actions that are more general in nature.

---

If this sounds a little confusing, don't worry (it is)! It'll become clearer as we practice. For now, to separate things out, we'll focus on the **preterite** (definite actions), and learn how to conjugate each of the regular verb types (-ar, -er, and -ir).

---

Later in this unit, we'll switch our attention to the **imperfect** (general actions) and do the same there.

Let's take a look at how to conjugate -ar verbs in the preterite!

---
Some examples:

|  **Spanish**  |  **English**  | 
| --------- | -------- |
| **hablar**  | to speak |
| **(yo) hablé** | I spoke |
| **(tú) hablaste** | you spoke |
| **(él/ella) habló** | he/she spoke | 
| **(nosotros) hablamos** | we spoke |
| **(ellos) hablaron** | they spoke |

---

The **preterite** is used only for actions that have a definite start and end. Those beginning and endpoints may or may not be stated explicitly. 

For example, if you're saying "I spoke with him about the llama.", you'd use the preterite, because your action is now complete (definite) and took place at a specific point in time, even though you didn't say it here.

---

You can think of the **preterite** as the regular past tense, since it encompasses what we would normally use in English, saying things like: "I ran," "she cooked," "the lawyer rode a purple giraffe in Nepal."

You know, just normal things you might say.

---

Let's take one last look at the endings for -ar verbs in the preterite:

|  **Pronoun**  |  **Ending**  | 
| --------- | -------- |
| **yo**  | -é |
| **tú** | -aste |
| **él/ella** | -ó | 
| **nosotros/nosotras** | -amos |
| **ellos/ellas** | -aron |

title: Judgment call
text:
The last situation we'll talk about in this unit is what's called an *impersonal opinion*. But wait, aren't all opinions personal?

Technically, yes. They do belong to a person. Perhaps a clearer distinction here would be to say that we're talking about *general, debatable opinions*.

---

If you say "I think that sushi is good," that's an *objective statement*. You're claiming it as your opinion by saying "I think" (or similarly, "I believe").

This tells us that this kind of statement should use the *indicative mood*. It is objectively your personal opinion.

---

What if you tweak your statement to say "It's great that you eat sushi"? Grammatically, this changes everything. Even though this is, of course, still your opinion, it goes from personal to *general*.

---

This kind of statement introduces an element of uncertainty and subjectivity, as it's a general statement that is now up for debate. Is it great, or is it not?

Because of this uncertainty, it lets us know we should use the subjunctive in this case.

---

Keep in mind that we're not talking about the intent behind the statements, merely about the grammar. If you say "I think..." or "I believe...", you're stating *for a fact* that this is your personal belief. It's clear that this is the truth.

---

If you say "It's important that...", you're introducing ambiguity. It could be important, or it could not. It's not clear, and that's where the subjunctive comes in.

---

Unlike many of the other situations we've talked about, it's more important to understand the structure of this kind of statement than to memorize specific phrases that tell us to use the subjunctive.

---

That being said, here are a few examples of the *types* of phrases that fit into this situation. Of course, we'll see more during the drills coming up.

- **es fantástico que** - it's fantastic that
- **es mejor que** - it's better that
- **es necesario que** - it's necessary that
- **es preferible que** - it's preferable that
- **es importante que** - it's important that
- **es ridículo que** - it's ridiculous that
- **es terrible que** - it's terrible that

---

And, naturally, negating all these results in the same situation. Whether you're saying **it's necessary that...** or **it's not necessary that...**, both will use the subjunctive.

title: Last but not least
text:
The last two irregular verbs that are important to know are **hacer** (*to do*) and **decir** (*to say*). These don't fit nicely into the other groups, so we'll just have to memorize how they work.

---

For **hacer**, the infinitive becomes simply **ha-**, and then we add the correct ending:

|  **Spanish**  |  **English**  |
| --------- | -------- |
| **hacer**  | to do |
| **(yo) haría** | I would do |
| **(tú) harías** | you would do |
| **(él/ella) haría** | he/she would do | 
| **(nosotros) haríamos** | we would do |
| **(ellos) harían** | they would do |

---

**Decir** is a similar story. The infinitive changes to **di-**, and then we tag on the proper ending.

|  **Spanish**  |  **English**  |
| --------- | -------- |
| **decir**  | to say |
| **(yo) diría** | I would say |
| **(tú) dirías** | you would say |
| **(él/ella) diría** | he/she would say | 
| **(nosotros) diríamos** | we would say |
| **(ellos) dirían** | they would say |

---

Let's practice these last two, and that'll be it for the conditional tense!

title: Let's count to 10
text:
One of the most important things we can learn early on is how to count and express quantities of things. That's right, it's time to learn our numbers!

---

Let's start by learning zero through ten:

0\. cero
1\. uno
2\. dos
3\. tres
4\. cuatro
5\. cinco
6\. seis
7\. siete
8\. ocho
9\. nueve
10\. diez

---

The only real way to learn numbers well is to use them in context, rather than just counting up and down. So, let's get to practicing!

title: Location, location, location
text:
One thing you'll probably want to be able to talk about early on as you meet new people is where you're from. Let's take a look at a quick example of a conversation covering this topic.

---

**¿De dónde eres?**
*Where are you from?*

**Soy de México. ¿Y tú?**
*I'm from Mexico. And you?*

**Soy de los Estados Unidos. Vivo en Nueva York.**
*I'm from the United States. I live in New York.*

---

Not too complicated, right? Don't worry about understanding every single word, exactly how all the verbs are working, or any of that right now.

We're simply trying to get familiar with some of these simple greetings, and you'll continue to see these as we go forward.

---

Here's some of the vocab that appears in this exchange:

|  **Spanish**  |  **English**  | 
| --------- | -------- |
| **dónde**  | where |
| **de**  | from |
| **soy**  | I am |
| **eres**  | you are |

---

Let's take one more look at this dialogue, this time just in Spanish.

**¿De dónde eres?**

**Soy de México. ¿Y tú?**

**Soy de los Estados Unidos. Vivo en Nueva York.**

---

Keep in mind that we'll introduce more place names (countries, states, cities, etc.) in upcoming lessons. Right now, it's mostly important to focus on the structure of the conversation.

title: Make do with what we have
More than one
text:
Remember the **infinitive** form of a verb? That's what we call the form you'd see in the dictionary, like **ser** (*to be*), **comer** (*to eat*), **hablar** (*to speak*), etc.

Well, for reflexive verbs, that infinitive includes the third-person reflexive pronoun on the end. For example: **llamarse** (*to call oneself*), **bañarse** (*to take a bath*), and **lavarse** (*to wash oneself*).

---

This is good to know, but it becomes especially relevant when there's more than one verb in a sentence. In these cases, you have two options: to include the pronoun ahead of the conjugated verb, or to place it at the end of the infinitive. 

Take a look at these sentences, which are identical in meaning:

**Me quiero bañar.**
**Quiero bañarme.**
*I want to take a bath.*

---

Here are a few more examples illustrating the concept:

**Nos queremos ver.**
**Queremos vernos.**
*We want to see ourselves.*

**Él se necesita lavar las manos.**
**Él necesita lavarse las manos.**
*He needs to wash his hands.*

**Ella no se puede dormir.**
**Ella no puede dormirse.**
*She can't fall asleep.*

title: Mucho y bueno
text:
Earlier, we said that most—but not all—adjectives in Spanish come *after* the nouns they're modifying (unlike English). Well, here come the exceptions!

---

Adjectives that have to do with **quantity** (including numbers) most often appear *before* the noun they're modifying.

|  **Spanish**  |  **English**  | 
| --------- | -------- |
|  **muchos libros**  | many books |
|  **mucha comida**  | a lot of food |
|  **pocos carros**  | few cars |
|  **unas sillas**  | some chairs |
|  **cinco minutos**  | five minutes |

---

**What comes before**

There are a couple of other common adjectives that often come before the nouns they modify. Bueno (*good*) and malo (*bad*) can both appear before nouns, which you'll see a lot.

---

When these adjectives come before a masculine noun, they drop the "-o" at the end of the word. Take a look at these examples:

- libro bueno -> **buen libro**
- comida buena -> **buena comida**
- libro malo -> **mal libro**
- comida mala -> **mala comida**

---

**Grande** (*big, large*) behaves a little differently when it comes before a noun. When it's *after* a noun, it means big, but *before* a noun, it changes to **gran** (if singular) and means *great.*

|  **Spanish**  |  **English**  | 
| --------- | -------- |
|  **un perro grande**  | a big dog |
|  **un gran perro**  | a great dog |
|  **un gran presidente**  | a great president |
|  **una gran mujer**  | a great woman |

---

**Best, worst, least**

The last category we'll talk about here is adjectives relating to a **value judgment** on a noun. If we're talking about the *best* or *worst* of a noun, then the adjective usually comes ahead of it.

|  **Spanish**  |  **English**  | 
| --------- | -------- |
|  **el mejor estudiante**  | the best student |
|  **la peor comida**  | the worst food |
|  **la menor cantidad**  | the least quantity |

title: One exception
text:
There's one key verb here that doesn't really play by the rules of the reflexive, and that is **ir** (*to go*). Its reflexive form is **irse**, and it means *to leave*.

**Yo voy a la oficina.**
*I go to the office.*

**Me voy de la oficina.**
*I leave from the office.*

---

There are a few other verbs that have slight changes of meaning when they switch their infinitive forms, but none are different enough to worry about here.

title: Not until I have my coffee
On one condition...
text:
The **conditional tense** is exactly what it sounds like: it gives us a way to talk about things that hypothetically *would* happen, if a certain condition is met.

Sometimes that condition is stated explicitly (i.e. I would go to the movies if I had money), and sometimes it's not stated at all (i.e. I would be interested).

---

In the most basic terms, you can think of the Spanish conditional tense as very similar to using "would" in English.

---

For example, here are a couple of basic uses of the conditional:

**Compraría ese libro, pero no tengo dinero.**
*I would buy that book, but I don't have money.*

**Me interesaría aprender más sobre México.**
*I would be interested in learning more about Mexico.*

---

Similar to the *simple future* tense, to conjugate the **conditional tense** we add the corresponding endings to the *infinitive* form of the verb. In other words, no need to drop the -ar, -er, or -ir.

Oh, and all three verb groups use the same endings!

---

Here are the endings for the conditional tense:

|  **Pronoun**  |  **Ending**  | 
| --------- | -------- |
| **yo**  | -ía |
| **tú** | -ías |
| **él/ella** | -ía | 
| **nosotros/nosotras** | -íamos |
| **ellos/ellas** | -ían |

---

Here's an example using the word **estudiar** (*to study*):

|  **Spanish**  |  **English**  | 
| --------- | -------- |
| **estudiar**  | to study |
| **(yo) estudiaría** | I would study |
| **(tú) estudiarías** | you would study |
| **(él/ella) estudiaría** | he/she would study | 
| **(nosotros) estudiaríamos** | we would study |
| **(ellos) estudiarían** | they would study |

---

And one more example with **ser** (*to be*) before we get to practicing:

|  **Spanish**  |  **English**  | 
| --------- | -------- |
| **ser**  | to be |
| **(yo) sería** | I would be |
| **(tú) serías** | you would be |
| **(él/ella) sería** | he/she would be | 
| **(nosotros) seríamos** | we would be |
| **(ellos) serían** | they would be |

title: One rule to rule them all
text:
Before we talk about our first use case for the subjunctive, let's learn how to conjugate it.

---

To conjugate verbs in the subjunctive, we start with what's called the **yo** form of the verb, which is the verb conjugated into the first-person present tense (hence the **yo**). 

Then, we drop the -o at the end to get the *stem*. Lastly, we add the proper ending.

---

For example:

- hablar -> hablo -> habl- -> **hable**
- escribir -> escribo -> escrib- -> **escriba**

We've conjugated a lot of verbs, so this should be old hat by now. The only difference is that we begin with the **yo** form instead of the infinitive.

---

For many verbs, the stem of the present tense *yo* will look exactly the same as the infinitive stem, so why make things more complicated? 

Well, it helps to think of subjunctive conjugation this way, because this one rule covers both regular and irregular verbs (with a couple of exceptions that we'll talk about later).

---

In other words, starting with the **yo** form and then dropping the -o works for verbs that have irregular **yo** forms as well. We just roll with it and add the proper ending from there, which makes everything simpler.

- comer -> como -> com- -> **coma**
- querer -> quiero -> quier- -> **quiera**

---

Okay, so what are the correct endings for the subjunctive? Well, here they are:

|  **pronoun** |  **-ar**  |  **-er, -ir**  | 
| --------- | -------- | -------- |
| yo | **-e** | **-a** |
| tú | **-es** | **-as** |
| él/ella | **-e** | **-a** |
| nosotros | **-emos** | **-amos** |
| ellos | **-en** | **-an** |

---

Here are some examples for each ending with verbs that have regular **yo** forms:

|  **hablar** |  **comer**  |  **escribir**  | 
| --------- | -------- | -------- |
| hable | coma | escriba |
| hables | comas | escribas |
| hable | coma | escriba |
| hablemos | comamos | escribamos |
| hablen | coman | escriban |

---

Finally, here are a few examples of verbs with irregular **yo** forms.

|  **pronoun** |  **tener**  |  **querer**  | 
| --------- | -------- | -------- |
| yo | **tenga** | **quiera** |
| tú | **tengas** | **quieras** |
| él/ella | **tenga** | **quiera** |
| nosotros | **tengamos** | **quieramos** |
| ellos | **tengan** | **quieran** |

---

For once, it's nice to see that there's a method to the madness when it comes to irregular verbs, and that there are rules we can follow instead of just memorizing them.

Let's talk about how the subjunctive is used to express desire, and then get some practice.

title: One, two, three strikes you're out
Other endings
text:
**Adjectives ending with "-e"**

So far we've gone over adjectives that end in "-o," but there are other endings as well, many of which we've seen in earlier lessons. One of the more common endings for adjectives in Spanish is "-e,"  and these words behave as follows:

|  **Spanish**  |  **English**  | 
| --------- | -------- |
|  **un hombre inteligente**  | an intelligent man |
|  **una mujer inteligente**  | an intelligent woman |
|  **los hombres inteligentes**  | the intelligent men |
|  **las mujeres inteligentes**  | the intelligent women |

---

Just like their noun counterparts, adjectives that end in "-e" have a singular and plural form to match the nouns they modify (just add an "s" to create the plural), but they don't take different forms for gender.

---

Instead, they are the same whether they're modifying a masculine or feminine noun. So for these adjectives, there are only two versions to remember:

- **inteligente**
- **inteligentes**

---

**Adjectives ending in consonants**

There are also many adjectives that end in consonants, and these behave largely the same as those that end in "-e." They have a singular and plural form but don't change for grammatical gender.

---

|  **Spanish**  |  **English**  | 
| --------- | -------- |
|  **un trabajo difícil**  | a difficult job |
|  **una clase difícil**  | a difficult class |
|  **los juegos difíciles**  | the difficult games |
|  **las preguntas difíciles**  | the difficult questions |

---

Again, with these adjectives ending in consonants, there are only two forms to remember:

- **difícil**
- **difíciles**

We make the plural by adding "-es" to the end of the word. The only exception here is when the adjective ends in a "z", in which case the "z" changes to "c" before adding "-es."

For example, **feliz** (*happy*) becomes **felices**.

---

Here are a few examples to take a look at before we jump into practicing some new words!

|  **Spanish**  |  **English**  | 
| --------- | -------- |
|  **una casa grande**  | a big house |
|  **un libro verde**  | a green book |
|  **los doctores interesantes**  | the interesting doctors |
|  **las niñas felices**  | the happy girls |
|  **un actor popular**  | a popular actor |
|  **los carros azules**  | the blue cars |

title: Overview
text:
There are three verb endings in Spanish: **-ar**, **-er**, and **-ir**.

We can conjugate any *regular* verb by dropping the ending (-ar, -er, or -ir), and then attaching a new ending depending on the subject.

---

Here are the **present tense** conjugation charts for regular verbs:

**-ar verbs**

|  **Pronoun**  |  **Ending**  | 
| --------- | -------- |
| yo  | -o |
| tú | -as |
| él/ella | -a | 
| nosotros/nosotras | -amos |
| ellos/ellas | -an |
| ustedes | -an |

---

**-er verbs**

|  **Pronoun**  |  **Ending**  | 
| --------- | -------- |
| yo  | -o |
| tú | -es |
| él/ella | -e | 
| nosotros/nosotras | -emos |
| ellos/ellas | -en |
| ustedes | -en |

---

**-ir verbs**

|  **Pronoun**  |  **Ending**  | 
| --------- | -------- |
| yo  | -o |
| tú | -es |
| él/ella | -e | 
| nosotros/nosotras | -imos |
| ellos/ellas | -en |
| ustedes | -en |

---

And here are some examples with full words:

|  **Spanish**  |  **English**  | 
| --------- | -------- |
| hablar  | to speak |
| (yo) hablo | I speak |
| (tú) hablas | you speak |
| (él/ella) habla | he/she speaks | 
| (nosotros/nosotras) hablamos | we speak |
| (ellos/ellas) hablan | they speak |
| (ustedes) hablan | you (all) speak |

---

|  **Spanish**  |  **English**  | 
| --------- | -------- |
| comer  | to eat |
| (yo) como | I eat |
| (tú) comes | you eat |
| (él/ella) come | he/she eats | 
| (nosotros/nosotras) comemos | we eat |
| (ellos/ellas) comen | they eat |
| (ustedes) comen | you (all) eat |

---

|  **Spanish**  |  **English**  | 
| --------- | -------- |
| escribir  | to write |
| (yo) escribo | I write |
| (tú) escribes | you write |
| (él/ella) escribe | he/she writes | 
| (nosotros/nosotras) escribimos | we write |
| (ellos/ellas) escriben | they write |
| (ustedes) escriben | you (all) write |

title: Passive voice
text:
This use is less common, just like in English, but we can also use the verb **ser** + *past participle* to express something in the passive voice.

---

For example:

**Las palabras son entendidas.**
*The words are understood.*

**La comida fue descubierto.**
*The food was discovered.*

---

If you'd like to talk about who performed an action using the passive voice, add in the word **por**, which, in this case, means "by".

**El libro fue escrito por el autor.**
*The book was written by the author.*

**La tarea es realizada por el estudiante.**
*The homework is done by the student.*

---

Obviously, this is an awkward way to speak, but it's important to make sure we can understand it! Let's practice, and then move onto more useful things.

title: Perfectly balanced
text:
In Spanish, we can combine the verb **haber** (*to have*) with the past participle to create the perfect tenses. In this lesson, we'll talk about the **present perfect**.

---

This should look familiar in English, as we use the perfect tense to talk about actions that are fully completed. In this case, we're talking about a state that refers to the present, to right now:

I **have eaten** the candy.

The student **has studied** for her test.

The kids **have played** that game.

---

The present perfect functions exactly the same in Spanish:

**He comido** los dulces.
*I **have eaten** the candy.*

El estudiante **ha estudiado** para el examen.
*The student **has studied** for the test.*

Los niños **han jugado** ese juego.
*The kids **have played** that game.*

---

Since we already know how to use the past participle, all we need to learn is how to conjugate **haber**.

|  **Spanish**  |  **English**  | 
| --------- | -------- |
| **haber**  | to have |
| **(yo) he** | I have |
| **(tú) has** | you have |
| **(él/ella) ha** | he/she has | 
| **(nosotros) hemos** | we have |
| **(ellos) han** | they have |

---

*Note: as per usual, because each conjugation is unique, we can generally leave off the pronoun before the verb.*

title: Practice makes progress
text:
Most courses would teach you past tense right about now, but not us! We'll cover past tense in the next section, but we figure that while we're talking about **estar**, we should discuss the **progressive tense** (because it's super useful).

---

Progressive tense is what we use to talk about actions that are *in progress*. It's the difference between "What do you do?" (present tense) and "What are you doing?" (progressive tense).

---

The plain old present tense is necessary, of course, but we often talk about things that are happening right now. 

For example, "I am eating cereal" and "I eat cereal" have completely different meanings.

---

To use the progressive tense in English, we add the ending **-ing** to the action verb: 

- eat -> **eating**
- run -> **running**
- speak -> **speaking**

and we precede the action with the verb "to be":

- I **am** eating
- She **is** running
- They **are**  speaking

---

Note here that the action word with the "-ing" ending (called the *participle* for those who care about grammatical terms) doesn't change at all. 

No matter who's performing the action, it remains the same. 

It's the "to be" in front of it that changes form depending on who is doing the action and when (past, present, future) it's taking place.

---

It's the same with Spanish! For the "to be" we use the verb **estar**, which changes form (conjugation) to tell us who we're talking about (and when, though we'll stick with the present for now), and the action word ("-ing" equivalent) stays the same no matter what. 

That means that there's less conjugation for us to learn. Yay!

---

In English, we add the ending "-ing" ending to verbs to create the progressive form. In Spanish, we conjugate the verb the same way we have before: removing the ending and adding a new one.

---

Let's take a look at the conjugations for our three types of Spanish verbs (-ar, -er, and -ir).

|  **Verb Type**  |  **New Ending**  |  **Example**  | 
| --------- | -------- | -------- |
| -ar  | -ando | hablando |
| -er  | -iendo | comiendo |
| -ir  | -iendo | escribiendo |

---

As you can see, these verbs always end in "-ndo," and there are only two conjugations to memorize, as the conjugation for "-er" and "-ir" verbs is the same! 

So to use the full progressive tense, all we do is add a conjugation of **estar** before this "-ndo" form, and we're rocking and rolling.

---

Here are some examples:

|  **Spanish**  |  **English**  | 
| --------- | -------- |
| **estoy comiendo** | I am eating |
| **estás comiendo** | you are eating |
| **(él/ella) está comiendo** | he/she is eating | 
| **estamos comiendo** | we are eating |
| **están comiendo** | they are eating |

---

And a few with different verbs:

|  **Spanish**  |  **English**  | 
| --------- | -------- |
| **estoy hablando** | I am talking/speaking |
| **estás escribiendo** | you are writing |
| **(él/ella) está corriendo** | he/she is running |
| **estamos cocinando** | we are cooking |
| **están estudiando** | they are studying |

Pretty useful, right?

title: In progress
text:
Progressive tense is what we use to talk about actions that are *in progress*. It's the difference between "What do you do?" (present tense) and "What are you doing?" (progressive tense).

For example, "I am eating cereal" and "I eat cereal" have completely different meanings.

---

To use the progressive tense in English, we add the ending **-ing** to the action verb: 

- eat -> **eating**
- run -> **running**
- speak -> **speaking**

and we precede the action with the verb "to be":

- I **am** eating
- She **is** running
- They **are**  speaking

---

Note here that the action word with the "-ing" ending (called the *participle* for those who care about grammatical terms) doesn't change at all. 

No matter who's performing the action, it remains the same. 

It's the "to be" in front of it that changes form depending on who is doing the action and when (past, present, future) it's taking place.

---

It's the same with Spanish! For the "to be" we use the verb **estar**, which changes its conjugation to tell us who we're talking about and when (though this pack is all about the *present progressive*), and the action word ("-ing" equivalent) stays the same no matter what. 

---

In English, we add the ending "-ing" ending to verbs to create the progressive form. In Spanish, we conjugate the verb the same way we have before: removing the ending and adding a new one.

---

Let's take a look at the conjugations for our three types of Spanish verbs (-ar, -er, and -ir).

|  **Verb Type**  |  **New Ending**  |  **Example**  | 
| --------- | -------- | -------- |
| -ar  | -ando | hablando |
| -er  | -iendo | comiendo |
| -ir  | -iendo | escribiendo |

---

As you can see, these verbs always end in "-ndo," and there are only two conjugations to memorize, as the conjugation for "-er" and "-ir" verbs is the same! 

So to use the full progressive tense, all we do is add a conjugation of **estar** before this "-ndo" form, and we're rocking and rolling.

---

Here are some examples:

|  **Spanish**  |  **English**  | 
| --------- | -------- |
| **estoy comiendo** | I am eating |
| **estás comiendo** | you are eating |
| **(él/ella) está comiendo** | he/she is eating | 
| **estamos comiendo** | we are eating |
| **están comiendo** | they are eating |

---

And a few with different verbs:

|  **Spanish**  |  **English**  | 
| --------- | -------- |
| **estoy hablando** | I am talking/speaking |
| **estás escribiendo** | you are writing |
| **(él/ella) está corriendo** | he/she is running |
| **estamos cocinando** | we are cooking |
| **están estudiando** | they are studying |

title: Putting it all together
text:
**100-199**

Even though 100 is "cien," it changes to "ciento" for 101-199. If there are just two words, it's simply **ciento + second number** (no "y" between):
100\. cien
101\. ciento uno
102\. ciento dos...
120\. ciento veinte
140\. ciento cuarenta
180\. ciento ochenta

---

For the rest, they work just like 1-99:
131\. ciento treinta y uno
157\. ciento cincuenta y siete
199\. ciento noventa y nueve

---

This is the same for all of the hundreds:
201\. doscientos uno
243\. doscientos cuarenta y tres
360\. trescientos sesenta
362\. trescientos sesenta y seis
911\. novecientos once
999\. novecientos noventa y nueve

title: Roaring twenties
text:
We mentioned previously that the twenties had an interesting quirk. Recall that with the numbers 16-19 we took two numbers (ten and a single digit) and smashed them into one (*diez y siete* -> **diecisiete**).

---

The twenties do the same thing, except all the way through from 21-29. So, they take the concept of saying "twenty and one" (veinte y uno) and combine them into one word: **veintiuno**. And the pattern continues with the rest.

---

20\. veinte
21\. veintiuno
22\. veintidos
23\. veintitres
24\. veinticuatro
25\. veinticinco
26\. veintiséis
27\. veintisiete
28\. veintiocho
29\. veintinueve

---

It's clear to see why this is the case. **Veinticinco** simply sounds like *veinte y cinco* said quickly, so it's a kind of shortcut.

The key thing to remember here (which is different from 30 and higher) is that the final "-e" in **veinte** changes to an "-i" and then you simply add the single digit to the end.

---

A quick note on veintiuno (twenty-one): just like other "ones," it changes form depending on the gender of the word it's describing.

For example:

**Un caballo, veintiún caballos**
*One horse, twenty-one horses*

**Una hora, veintiuna horas**
*One hour, twenty-one hours*

---

Pay attention to the masculine form here, it has a tricky accent mark: **veintiún**

title: Simple, but effective
text:
You can think of the **simple future** basically as a different way to say the same thing. For example, take a look at these two sentences in English:

**I am going to eat the food.**

**I will eat the food.**

There might be a slight difference in connotation, but they basically have the same meaning. The same is true of these two methods of expressing the future in Spanish.

---

Let's see this in action by adding in the Spanish translations for those two examples:

**Voy a comer la comida.**
*I am going to eat the food.*

**Comeré la comida.**
*I will eat the food.*

---

Here are the endings for the simple future conjugation. Unlike the present and past tense, we simply add these endings to the end of the *infinitive form* of the verb. 

Oh, and these endings apply to all three regular verb groups, which is great for us!

|  **Pronoun**  |  **Ending**  | 
| --------- | -------- |
| **yo**  | -é |
| **tú** | -ás |
| **él/ella** | -á | 
| **nosotros/nosotras** | -emos |
| **ellos/ellas** | -án |

---

And here's an example using the word **ganar** (*to win*):

|  **Spanish**  |  **English**  | 
| --------- | -------- |
| **ganar**  | to win |
| **(yo) ganaré** | I will win |
| **(tú) ganarás** | you will win |
| **(él/ella) ganará** | he/she will win | 
| **(nosotros) ganaremos** | we will win |
| **(ellos) ganarán** | they will win |

title: Outlaws & renegades
text:
We've already talked about how *most* irregular verbs fit nicely into the subjunctive with no special consideration.

But, as per usual, there are a few important verbs that like to do their own thing, so let's talk about those outlaws.

---

There are six verbs we'll talk about here: 
- **ir** (*to go*)
- **ser** (*to be*)
- **estar** (the other *to be*)
- **dar** (*to give*)
- **saber** (*to know*)
- **haber** (*to exist*)

---

Let's look at the first three, **ir**, **ser**, and **estar**:

|  **ir** |  **ser**  |  **estar**  | 
| --------- | -------- | -------- |
| vaya | sea | esté |
| vayas | seas | estés |
| vaya | sea | esté |
| vayamos | seamos | estémos |
| vayan | sean | estén |

*Note: pay attention to the accent that shows up for estar here.*

---

Now for the others, **dar**, **saber**, and **haber**:

|  **dar** |  **saber**  |  **haber**  | 
| --------- | -------- | -------- |
| dé | sepa | haya |
| des | sepas | hayas |
| dé | sepa | haya |
| demos | sepamos | hayamos |
| den | sepan | hayan |

*Note that the accent for dar is only for the first- and third-person conjugations.*

---

For these six, unfortunately, we will have to just learn them through practice, so let's get to it!

title: Slowly I Turned
text:
Step by step and inch by inch, we're getting there, so pat yourself on the back for making it to Intermediate! Now we move on to simple adverbs, which is a good way to ease into some of the more challenging aspects of Spanish.

---

Expressing most simple Spanish adverbs falls into two camps: adding **-mente** to the end of feminine singular adjectives, or using the preposition **con** before the singular form of the noun. Let's take a look at some examples. First, **-mente** which you can think of as the **-ly** ending in English.

---

**rápida** -> **rápidamente**
*quick* -> *quickly*

**lenta** -> **lentamente**
*slow* -> *slowly*

**facil** -> **facilmente**
*easy* -> *easily*

**desesperada** -> **desesperadamente**
*desperate* -> *desperately*

**final** -> **finalmente**
*final* -> *finally*

---

*Note: If the adjective has an accent, the adverb will as well, such as in the previous example of rápida/rápidamente*

---

If that ever trips you up, there's a handy failsafe, which is the **con** + noun format. This can be used if you're having trouble recalling or spelling the feminine version of an adjective, or simply because certain adverbs can be a bit awkward when following the **-mente** rule.

---

pacientemente = **con paciencia**
*patiently*

respetuosamente = **con respeto**
*respectfully*

inteligentemente = **con inteligencia**
*intelligently*

dulcemente = **con dulzura**
*sweetly*

frecuentemente = **con frecuencia**
*frequently*

---

As we mentioned earlier, these two rules cover *most* simple adverbs, not all. Some adverbs simply don't have a pattern, such as **nunca** (never) and **a veces** (sometimes), which means you'll have to commit them to memory.

---

Never fear, though, we'll be covering some of these adverbs in the next lesson and beyond.

title: Something concrete - the preterite
text:
Unlike English, Spanish has two distince past tenses. These are called the **preterite** and the **imperfect**. Let's talk about the first one, the **preterite**.

---

The **preterite** is used for actions that are completed, that have a definite beginning and end. If you can define a specific time (or length of time) that you did something or a specific duration that the action lasted (even if you don't actually mention it in the sentence, you should use the **preterite**.

---

In English, this is the difference between saying **I cooked steak last night** (*the preterite*) and **I used to cook steak often** (*the imperfect*).

You can see that the first one has a specific beginning and end to the action of cooking, whereas the second just references something general about the past.

---

Just like the present tense, we can conjugate any *regular* verb using the **preterite** by dropping the ending (-ar, -er, or -ir), and then attaching a new ending depending on the subject.

---

Here are the **past tense** conjugation charts using the **preterite** form for regular verbs:

**-ar verbs**

|  **Pronoun**  |  **Ending**  | 
| --------- | -------- |
| **yo**  | -é |
| **tú** | -aste |
| **él/ella** | -ó | 
| **nosotros/nosotras** | -amos |
| **ellos/ellas** | -aron |

---

**-er and -ir verbs**

|  **Pronoun**  |  **Ending**  | 
| --------- | -------- |
| **yo**  | -í |
| **tú** | -iste |
| **él/ella** | -ió | 
| **nosotros/nosotras** | -imos |
| **ellos/ellas** | -ieron |


---

And here are some examples with full words:

|  **Spanish**  |  **English**  | 
| --------- | -------- |
| **hablar**  | to speak |
| **(yo) hablé** | I spoke |
| **(tú) hablaste** | you spoke |
| **(él/ella) habló** | he/she spoke | 
| **(nosotros) hablamos** | we spoke |
| **(ellos) hablaron** | they spoke |

---

|  **Spanish**  |  **English**  | 
| --------- | -------- |
| **comer**  | to eat |
| **(yo) comí** | I ate |
| **(tú) comiste** | you ate |
| **(él/ella) comió** | he/she ate | 
| **(nosotros) comimos** | we ate |
| **(ellos) comieron** | they ate |

---

|  **Spanish**  |  **English**  | 
| --------- | -------- |
| **vivir**  | to live |
| **(yo) viví** | I lived |
| **(tú) viviste** | you lived |
| **(él/ella) vivió** | he/she lived | 
| **(nosotros) vivimos** | we lived |
| **(ellos) vivieron** | they lived |

title: Start here
text:
For positive commands in Spanish (meaning that we're telling someone *to do* something), we use the **third person present tense** form of the verb.

---

For example:

**Toma la foto.**
*Take the photo.*

**Come la comida.**
*Eat the food.*

**Escribe el libro.**
*Write the book.*

---

For negative commands—telling someone *not to do* something—we use the second-person subjunctive in the **tú** conjugation.

---

Here are a few more examples using the same verbs as before:

**No tomes la foto.**
*Don't take the photo.*

**No comas la comida.**
*Do not eat the food.*

**No escribas el libro.**
*Don't write the book.*

title: Teen spirit
text:
Now it's time to tackle the teens. Let's learn the numbers 11-19.

---

**Teens: 11-19**
11\. once
12\. doce
13\. trece
14\. catorce
15\. quince
16\. dieciséis
17\. diecisiete
18\. dieciocho
19\. diecinueve

---

You'll notice something curious here. The numbers 11-15 follow a different format than 16-19 (and, as we'll see in just a bit, all the other numbers up to 100).

16-19 should be pretty clear. We take **diez** (10) and add the regular number to it. When this happens, instead of being "diez y séis" (ten and six), it becomes **dieciséis** (sixteen).

---

So, why the different format with 11-15? Well, it's mostly for historical reasons. In fact, most of the romance languages have this quirk, because they all inherited it from Latin (thanks, Latin)...

That just means we have to memorize those five numbers. With a little practice, this should be no big deal.

---

For now, other than those few, remember that as we get to bigger numbers, we first count by tens, then add the proper single-digit number to the end. This way of thinking will come in handy in the next few sections.

title: That's a negative
text:
So we know how to tell someone to do something, but what about when we need to tell them *not* to do something?

In that case, we actually switch to the second-person subjunctive, using the **tú** conjugation.

---

Here are a few examples:

**No tomes la foto.**
*Don't take the photo.*

**No comas la comida.**
*Do not eat the food.*

**No escribas el libro.**
*Don't write the book.*

---

Since we already learned the subjunctive, this should be pretty straightforward. The nice thing about the imperative is that there are no new conjugations to learn, mostly just forms we've seen before being used in slightly different ways.

---

As with everything, practice makes progress, so let's get to it!

title: That's not how the Force works!
The future is simple
text:
Okay, so now that we know how to use the **informal future** to express what we *are going* to do, let's learn how to conjugate verbs for the **simple future**.

*Note: keep in mind that **informal future** (using **ir + a + infinitive**) is used more often than the simple future, so when in doubt, default to the informal.*

---

You can think of the **simple future** as just a different way to say the same thing. For example, take a look at these two sentences in English:

**I am going to eat the food.**

**I will eat the food.**

There might be a slight difference in connotation, but they basically have the same meaning, right? The same is true of these two methods of expressing the future in Spanish.

---

Let's add the Spanish translations to the previous example:

**Voy a comer la comida.**
*I am going to eat the food.*

**Comeré la comida.**
*I will eat the food.*

Not too crazy, right?

---

Let's look at the endings for the simple future conjugation. Unlike the present and past tense, we simply add these endings to the end of the *infinitive form* of the verb. 

Oh, and these endings apply to all three regular verb groups, which makes it easy for us!

|  **Pronoun**  |  **Ending**  | 
| --------- | -------- |
| **yo**  | -é |
| **tú** | -ás |
| **él/ella** | -á | 
| **nosotros/nosotras** | -emos |
| **ellos/ellas** | -án |

---

And here's an example using the word **estudiar** (*to study*):

|  **Spanish**  |  **English**  | 
| --------- | -------- |
| **estudiar**  | to study |
| **(yo) estudiaré** | I will study |
| **(tú) estudiarás** | you will study |
| **(él/ella) estudiará** | he/she will study | 
| **(nosotros) estudiaremos** | we will study |
| **(ellos) estudiarán** | they will study |

Okay, let's practice!

title: The right conditions
text:
In the most basic terms, you can think of the Spanish conditional tense as very similar to actions using the word "would" in English.

---

For example, here are a couple of basic uses of the conditional:

**Compraría ese libro, pero no tengo dinero.**
*I would buy that book, but I don't have money.*

**Me interesaría aprender más sobre México.**
*I would be interested in learning more about Mexico.*

---

To conjugate the **conditional tense**, we add the corresponding endings to the *infinitive* form of the verb. In other words, no need to drop the -ar, -er, or -ir.

Oh, and all three verb groups use the same endings, which is very convenient.

---

Here are the endings for the conditional tense:

|  **Pronoun**  |  **Ending**  | 
| --------- | -------- |
| **yo**  | -ía |
| **tú** | -ías |
| **él/ella** | -ía | 
| **nosotros/nosotras** | -íamos |
| **ellos/ellas** | -ían |

*Note the accents here!*

---

Here's an example using the word **estudiar** (*to study*):

|  **Spanish**  |  **English**  | 
| --------- | -------- |
| **estudiar**  | to study |
| **(yo) estudiaría** | I would study |
| **(tú) estudiarías** | you would study |
| **(él/ella) estudiaría** | he/she would study | 
| **(nosotros) estudiaríamos** | we would study |
| **(ellos) estudiarían** | they would study |

---

And another example with **ser** (*to be*):

|  **Spanish**  |  **English**  | 
| --------- | -------- |
| **ser**  | to be |
| **(yo) sería** | I would be |
| **(tú) serías** | you would be |
| **(él/ella) sería** | he/she would be | 
| **(nosotros) seríamos** | we would be |
| **(ellos) serían** | they would be |

---

One more example with **escribir** (*to write*):

|  **Spanish**  |  **English**  | 
| --------- | -------- |
| **escribir**  | to write |
| **(yo) escribiría** | I would write |
| **(tú) escribirías** | you would write |
| **(él/ella) escribiría** | he/she would write | 
| **(nosotros) escribiríamos** | we would write |
| **(ellos) escribirían** | they would write |

title: The Time is Now
text:
With adverbs of place behind us, we can now move on to adverbs of time. You can think of these as answers to the questions "When?" or "How often?" In English, these are words like now, tomorrow, or weekly. Let's take a look.

---

|  **Adverb**  |  **English**  |
| -------- | -------- |
|  **hoy**  |  today  |
|  **mañana**  |  tomorrow  |
|  **ayer**  |  yesterday  |
|  **anoche**  |  last night  |
|  **anteanoche**  |  the night before last  |
|  **anteayer**  |  the day before yesterday  |

---

|  **Adverb**  |  **English**  |
| -------- | -------- |
|  **ahora**  |  now  |
|  **luego**  |  later  |
|  **tarde**  |  late  |
|  **todavía**  |  still  |
|  **ya**  |  already  |
|  **nunca**  |  never  |
|  **siempre**  |  always  |

---

There are a few other adverbs of time to make note of, but thankfully these follow the **-mente** suffix rule that applied previously. 

---

|  **Adverb**  |  **English**  |
| -------- | -------- |
|  **previamente**  |  previously  |
|  **recientemente**  |  recently  |
|  **actualmente**  |  currently  |
|  **brevemente**  |  briefly  |
|  **diariamente**  |  daily  |
|  **ocasionalmente**  |  occasionally  |

title: There would be more...
text:
In the second group of irregular verbs, we replace the final vowel in the infinitive with **d** and add the correct ending:

So, for example, **salir** (*to leave*) would become **saldría** in the first and third person.

---

Let's look at the full conjugation chart for **salir**:

|  **Spanish**  |  **English**  | 
| --------- | -------- |
| **salir**  | to leave |
| **(yo) saldría** | I would leave |
| **(tú) saldrías** | you would leave |
| **(él/ella) saldría** | he/she would leave | 
| **(nosotros) saldríamos** | we would leave |
| **(ellos) saldrían** | they would leave |

---

And here are all the verbs in this group:

|  **Infinitive**  | **Meaning** | **Conditional**  | 
| --------- | -------- | -------- |
| salir  | to leave | **saldría** |
| poner  | to put | **pondría** |
| tener  | to have | **tendría** |
| venir  | to come | **vendría** |
| valer  | to be worth | **valdría** |

title: Not the droids you're looking for
This is highly irregular
text:
There are some important verbs that are irregular in the past tense, so (unfortunately) you just have to memorize their conjugations, just like we did with the present tense.

---

The bad news is that some of the most common verbs are irregular, but the good news (at least for the preterite form) is that they have some nice consistency between the conjugations, in that they generally follow the normal endings (they just happen to differ from their infinitives in weird ways).

---

Let's first take a look at **ser** (*to be*) and **ir** *(to go)*. In an excellent—but often confusing—turn of luck for us as learners, these two have the *exact same conjugations* in the preterite.

---

|  **Pronoun**  |  **ser** *(to be)*  |  **ir** *(to go)*  | 
| --------- | -------- | -------- |
| **yo**  | fui | fui |
| **tú** | fuiste | fuiste |
| **él/ella** | fue | fue | 
| **nosotros/nosotras** | fuimos | fuimos |
| **ellos/ellas** | fueron | fueron |

---

So, how do we tell these apart, then? For the most part, context!

**Fuimos estudiantes.**
*We were students.*

**Fuimos a la playa.**
*We went to the beach.*

---

Not too crazy, right?

*Note: if you're going **to** somewhere, you use the preposition "a" between the verb (ir) and the place you're going or went. For example, "Fuiste **a** la universidad" (You went **to** the university) or "Voy **a** la tienda" (I go **to** the store).*

title: Those other endings
text:
Now that we know how the preterite works, and we've done some practice with -ar verbs, let's go over how to conjugate -er and -ir verbs in the preterite.

---

Fortunately for us, they're both the same!

*(Note: as long as they're regular. Remember that a bunch of -ir verbs in particular tend to be irregular. We'll talk in-depth about common irregular verbs later.)*

---

Since these two are the same, let's take a look at the endings first, and then some specific examples next.

|  **Pronoun**  |  **Ending**  | 
| --------- | -------- |
| **yo**  | -í |
| **tú** | -iste |
| **él/ella** | -ió | 
| **nosotros/nosotras** | -imos |
| **ellos/ellas** | -ieron |

---

And now for an example of an -er verb:

|  **Spanish**  |  **English**  | 
| --------- | -------- |
| **comer**  | to eat |
| **(yo) comí** | I ate |
| **(tú) comiste** | you ate |
| **(él/ella) comió** | he/she ate | 
| **(nosotros) comimos** | we ate |
| **(ellos) comieron** | they ate |

---

Here's one with an -ir verb:

|  **Spanish**  |  **English**  | 
| --------- | -------- |
| **vivir**  | to live |
| **(yo) viví** | I lived |
| **(tú) viviste** | you lived |
| **(él/ella) vivió** | he/she lived | 
| **(nosotros) vivimos** | we lived |
| **(ellos) vivieron** | they lived |

---

Remember the key point that the preterite is used for concrete actions.

title: To cone a phrase
text:
The finish line is in sight! You've learned the rules that *most* adverbs follow, as well as adverbs of place, time, quantity, and manner, and now we're going to wrap things up with commonly used adverbial phrases. 

These phrases can help with context, as well as connotation, and can sometimes serve as a segue between thoughts. Let's take a look.

---

|  **Adverb**  |  **English**  |
| -------- | -------- |
|  **a veces**  |  sometimes  |
|  **al final**  |  in the end  |
|  **a tiempo**  |  on time  |
|  **a la vez**  |  at the same time  |
|  **de verdad**  |  really / honestly  |
|  **por fin**  |  finally  |

---

|  **Adverb**  |  **English**  |
| -------- | -------- |
|  **al principio**  |  in the beginning / initially  |
|  **en serio**  |  really / seriously  |
|  **de inmediato**  |  immediately  |
|  **de nuevo**  |  start over  |
|  **a menudo**  |  often  |
|  **de repente**  |  suddenly  |

---

Congratulations on navigating the many pockets of Spanish adverbs! 

You'll now be able to provide valuable context when communicating, such as time and place, as well as use handy phrases that ensure your message is as direct as possible. ¡Por fin!

title: Up, Down, and Around
text:
Now that you know some of the rules regarding adverbs, we're ready to disregard them completely as we move on to some of the loose-cannon adverbs that don't play by the rules. With these, you'll simply have to commit them to memory, but through practice it'll become second-nature in no time. We'll start with adverbs of place here.

---

Adverbs of place are usually used when answering the question of "Where?" as it provides information on location. In English, these would be words such as here, there, above, and below. Let's take a look.

---

|  **Adverb**  |  **English**  |
| -------- | -------- |
|  **aquí**  |  here  |
|  **acá**  |  over here  |
|  **allí**  |  there  |
|  **allá**  |  over there  |
|  **cerca**  |  near  |
|  **lejos**  |  far  |

---

|  **Adverb**  |  **English**  |
| -------- | -------- |
|  **delante**  |  in front  |
|  **detrás**  |  in rear  |
|  **encima**  |  on top  |
|  **debajo**  |  underneath  |
|  **dentro**  |  in  |
|  **fuera**  |  out  |

---

|  **Adverb**  |  **English**  |
| -------- | -------- |
|  **adelante**  |  ahead  |
|  **atrás**  |  behind  |
|  **arriba**  |  up/above  |
|  **abajo**  |  down/below  |
|  **adentro**  |  inside  |
|  **afuera**  |  outside  |

---

*Note: As you've probably noticed, a few of these words are extremely similar, both in spelling and definition. We've tried to give you the best context (i.e. **detrás** meaning in rear as it applies more to placement and **atrás** meaning behind as it applies more to movement) but the words are highly interchangeable, so don't lose too much sleep over it!*

title: We used to talk
text:
Now that we know *when* to use the imperfect, let's take a look at how to conjugate -ar verbs for it.

---

Here are the endings for the imperfect conjugation of -ar verbs:

|  **Pronoun**  |  **Ending**  | 
| --------- | -------- |
| **yo**  | -aba |
| **tú** | -abas |
| **él/ella** | -aba | 
| **nosotros/nosotras** | -abamos |
| **ellos/ellas** | -aban |

---

And here's an example using the word **hablar** (*to speak/talk*):

|  **Spanish**  |  **English**  | 
| --------- | -------- |
| **hablar**  | to speak |
| **(yo) hablaba** | I spoke |
| **(tú) hablabas** | you spoke |
| **(él/ella) hablaba** | he/she spoke | 
| **(nosotros) hablabamos** | we spoke |
| **(ellos) hablaban** | they spoke |

title: What to do, what to do
What are you going to do?
